newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: FEATURE-Islam makes troubled return in ex-Soviet Uzbekistan.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Islam makes troubled return in ex-Soviet Uzbekistan.

text.p: Women in shifts and leggings printed with geometric lines of dazzling blue, red and gold crowded around the grey stone tomb of a mediaeval Sufi saint.

The tomb and the curved stone roofs of the surrounding mosques have lured pilgrims for centuries since Bakhautdin Naqshband founded a secretive Moslem brotherhood near Uzbekistan's holy city of Bukhara in the 14th century.

In Soviet times, few would dare to gather here for worship. But today, the thousands of believers filing around Naqshband's shrine show Islam flourishing in Uzbekistan, having leapt up from the underground after 70 years of Soviet rule.
ISLAM DRIVEN UNDERGROUND
The Red Army crushed Central Asia's Moslem Basmachi guerrillas in the 1920s after the Bolshevik revolution in Russia.
The Soviets did not dare to destroy Naqshband's tomb, turning it instead into an anti-religious museum. But Communist attempts to turn the Uzbeks into atheists drove Islam underground.
"Before, the Soviet authorities were against us," said Bobojon Rakhmonov, 43, the imam in charge of the shrine.
"At that time, nobody would come here," he said, dressed in a grey tunic and white cap. "During Communist times, if party members came here to pray, they were expelled from the party."
The Sufi brotherhoods, like the Naqshbandiya, were able to keep the faith without mosques, keeping Islam alive in Uzbek apartments and houses.
Religious traditions -- Moslem marriage ceremonies, burials and circumcision -- were performed in secret, also observed by most Uzbek Communist officials.
Rakhmonov himself was trained quietly at home to be a religious leader. "My father and grandfather were religious people. I learned everything from them," he said.
LUCKY HAIRCUTS
A large pinch of superstition is mixed with strong belief at the tomb.

A father holding his baby son and clutching a pair of scissors approached Rakhmonov and asked shyly if he would cut his boy's hair. A first haircut from an imam is believed to bring fortune and wisdom to the boy in later life.

"This is bad -- they are believing in the stones and not in God," Makhmud, 15, said of the pilgrims who brushed their palms against the side of the tomb and then brought their hands down across their faces.
Pilgrims walked around the tomb three times anti-clockwise for good luck. Women hoping for a baby crawled under the trunk of a sacred tree nearby to improve their chances.
A cleric squatted under the shade of a mulberry tree out of the heat and recited pilgrims' prayer requests.
Even Makhmud, wearing an LA Lakers baseball cap, was not immune. Holding a plastic bottle of holy water, he said sheepishly: "My mother said I should wash with this as it will get rid of my spots."
TALEBAN MAKE UZBEK LEADER NERVOUS

But resurgent Islam in Uzbekistan, where the number of mosques has grown from 80 in 1991 to about 5,000 today, has made the desert nation's former Communist Party chief and current president, Islam Karimov, nervous.
"The Sufis say 'hearts with God, hands at work' -- this is a logic our president approves of," said Rakhmonov. He says he has experienced no government interference.
The president made the "haj", or pilgrimage to Mecca, shortly after independence in 1992, and Islam plays an important part in forging the Central Asian state's post-Soviet identity.

But Karimov has railed against the mediaeval Islam of the purist Taleban militia in neighbouring Afghanistan. He fears the Taleban could light a fundamentalist fire among his own 23 million population, hit hard by the government's mired economic reforms.
"The Taleban is making the government more nervous about things," said a Western diplomat in the Uzbek capital Tashkent.
Several mosques and religious schools which the authorities suspected of harbouring fundamentalist clerics have been shut.
Human rights groups say 20 Islamic clerics now languish in Uzbek prisons.
FEARS OF ALGERIAN SCENARIO
"There also appears to be a campaign against the hejab (veil) in Tashkent, begun unbelievably during Ramadan," said the diplomat, referring to the Moslem month of fasting between dawn and dusk.
"The hejab is being pulled off girls at school -- this is making ordinary people angry and the government is creating a big problem where there isn't one," he said.
Karimov has dealt ruthlessly with secular opposition groups but there is little he can do about Islam. Even if he closes the mosques, their Sufi traditions mean Uzbeks can simply return underground.
Independent-minded clerics, particularly in the eastern Ferghana Valley where Islamic traditions run deep, ignore the dictates of the government's Soviet-style "spiritual board" in Tashkent.
Observers worry that Karimov's clampdown could lead to a violent divide between the secular and the religious, as in Algeria and Egypt.

Rakhmonov attended to a crowd of pilgrims from neighbouring Kyrgyzstan, in pointed, white felt hats. Outside his stone courtyard, Uzbeks crawled over a holy well to try to scoop up a few drops of the precious water.
"Since independence, Sufism is stronger, and there are many adepts now," he said quietly.
